Narrative: The Board of County Commissioners (BCC) is the legislative and policy-making body of County government. Representatives from five Walton County districts are elected countywide and serve four year terms. The BCC establishes policies through the enactment of ordinances and adoption of resolutions, as well as appoints the County Administrator, Chief Financial Officer, and County Attorney. The BCC adopts the budget and makes all budget decisions regarding appropriation of funds to County departments, divisions, and Constitutional offices, in accordance with Florida State statutes.

The Clerk of Courts & County Comptroller is a separately elected Constitutional Officer of the County. The Clerk also acts as the Clerk to the Board of County Commissioners. As Clerk of the Court, areas of support for the judicial functions within the County include the Civil Division, Family Services, Felony Division, Jury Administration, Juvenile and Recording Divisions. Departments under the Clerk to the Board function include Finance, Information Systems and BCC recording. Services provided encompass accounting and auditing services, disbursements on contracts and purchases, investment of funds for the Board, information systems support (hardware and software) for court and accounting services and maintaining the “Official Records” for the Board. 

The Clerk’s budget, included in the County’s General Fund, is that portion of the operations not covered by fees charged for public services. Once the budget is approved, the Constitutional Office acts as a separate entity, setting its own policies and procedures, employee hiring and line-item budget management.

The Property Appraiser is a separately elected Constitutional Officer of the County. The Office’s budget is approved by the State Department of Revenue. Florida law requires the Board of County Commissioners to pay for the municipalities’ and school board’s cost of the Property Appraiser’s budget. This Office is responsible for determining the value of all property within the County, maintaining certain records connected with that responsibility and determining the tax on taxable property after taxes have been levied. The Office is also responsible for distributing the Truth-in-Millage (TRIM) notices.  

The Property Appraiser Office is operated as a separate entity, setting its own policies and procedures, employee hiring and line-item budget management.

The Sheriff is a separately elected Constitutional Officer of the County. Functions under the Sheriff include Corrections, Court Services, Law Enforcement, Animal Services, and Fire Rescue. The Corrections division operates the County detention facility, which involves inmate housing, medical services, food services, and prisoner transportation. The Court Services area provides bailiffs, courtroom security, and general jury/judicial protective services to the County courts. The Law enforcement function includes uniformed road patrol, criminal investigations, crime scene investigations, K-9 units, and the E911 Communications Center. Additionally, the Walton County Sheriff's Office has taken on other responsibilities, including the operations of the animal control facility and units, and the operations of Walton County Fire Rescue Services within the county. 

The Sheriff’s Office operates as a separate entity setting its policies and procedures, employee hiring, and line-item budget management.

The Supervisor of Elections is a separately elected Constitutional Officer of the County. The Office’s overall budget is included in the General Fund. Fee charges to the County’s various taxing authorities are based on a legislated percentage of taxes collected for each authority. The Office’s primary responsibilities are as an agent of state government. As an agent of Highway Safety and Motor Vehicles, the office administers titling and registration for vehicles and vessels. It issues hunting and fishing licenses as agent for Game and Fish Commission. In collecting sales tax on vehicle and vessel sales, the office is an agent for the Department of Revenue. The collection, investing and distribution of real and tangible taxes and the subsequent activities to collect delinquent taxes are as an agent of local and state government as is the collection of occupational license tax. 

The Tax Collector’s is operated as a separate entity setting its own policies and procedures, employee hiring and line-item budget management.

The Walton County Health Department operates as a full-time public health unit under a contractual agreement between Walton County and the State of Florida. In accordance with Chapter 154 of the Florida Statutes, counties are responsible for establishing and maintaining county health departments and public health facilities. These departments are tasked with delivering essential public health services, including maternal and child health, communicable disease control, and environmental health programs. 

County health departments (CHDs) improve the health status of the population by preventing epidemics, protecting against environmental hazards, encouraging healthy behaviors, preparing for and responding to disasters, and ensuring the quality and accessibility of health services.

CHDs in all 67 Florida counties—including Walton—function as state-local partnerships. They enter into an annual core contract with their host Board of County Commissioners, specifying the public health services to be provided and identifying the funding sources. These services are supported by a combination of state, county, and federal funds, as well as revenues from service fees, Medicaid, grants, and other contracts.

Effective public health delivery depends on coordinated local and regional partnerships. As stated in Section 154.001, Florida Statutes, “It is the intent of the Legislature to promote, protect, maintain and improve the health and safety of all citizens and visitors of our state through a system of coordinated county health department services.”

The Building Construction and Maintenance Department includes the Facilities Maintenance, Custodian, and Parks Maint. The Parks Division maintains the grounds of parks, ballfields, County office building lawns, community centers, irrigation at parks and office buildings, fencing, playground equipment, parking lot islands, and others. The Custodian Division provides cleaning services to County offices Countrywide.

The Building Department plays a pivotal role in ensuring the safety, compliance, and integrity of construction projects within our community. It serves as the central hub for regulatory oversight and support throughout the construction process. Among its core responsibilities, the department issues contractor licenses, reviews permit applications, and conducts thorough inspections at various stages of construction to guarantee adherence to building codes and standards.

The primary function of Code Compliance is to uphold and enhance the aesthetics, property values, health and safety, and overall quality of life for the residents and visitors of Walton County. This is achieved through the fair, consistent, and equitable enforcement of codes, regulations, and ordinances. By diligently ensuring adherence to established standards, Code Compliance plays a vital role in preserving the visual appeal and structural integrity of properties, safeguarding public health and safety, and fostering a harmonious and thriving community environment. Through their dedicated efforts, the department strives to maintain a high standard of living and a welcoming atmosphere for all who live in or visit Walton County.

Administration is responsible for executing the directives and priorities set forth by the Board of County Commissioners (BCC), ensuring efficient and effective governance within Walton County. Acting as the central hub of communication and coordination, Administration serves as the primary interface for the Citizens of Walton County, offering accessibility and responsiveness to their concerns, queries, and needs. 

In addition to facilitating citizen engagement, Administration functions as a supportive backbone for all county departments, offering crucial assistance and resources to ensure smooth operations across various sectors. By providing administrative support, guidance, and oversight, Administration helps departments optimize their functions, streamline processes, and achieve their respective objectives in alignment with the broader county goals. 

Furthermore, Administration serves as a vital link between the Board of County Commissioners and the constitutional offices and municipalities within Walton County. Acting as a liaison, it fosters collaboration, communication, and coordination among these entities, facilitating the exchange of information, resources, and initiatives to promote synergy and coherence in governance efforts.

Through its multifaceted roles, Administration plays a crucial part in upholding transparency, accountability, and responsiveness in county governance, ultimately contributing to the well-being and prosperity of Walton County and its residents.

Dept_Name: Eagle Springs Golf and Recreation Center
Narrative:
Walton County owns one golf course: Eagle Springs Golf and Recreation Center. The Board of County Commissioners purchased this course in 2019 with the goal of providing economic development and enhancing the quality of life for our residents and visitors through sports and recreation. Eagle Springs consists of 190 acres of property that contains an 18 hole golf course, as well as four spring fed lakes. This course is managed by the County with the goal of providing both citizens and visitors excellent recreational opportunities at affordable rates, while embracing the integrity of the game. More than 30,000 rounds of golf are played annually on this course. Eagle Springs provides additional amenities, including a driving range and a pro golf shop. Other recreational opportunities are also available, including pickleball courts, a public swimming pool, and a walking path around the perimeter of the golf course.

Eagle Springs provides additional amenities, including a driving range and a pro golf shop. Other recreational opportunities are also available, including pickleball courts, a public swimming pool, and a walking path around the perimeter of the golf course.

Eagle Springs Grill strives on providing exceptional service to the community, and ensuring quality food is produced for all patrons of the community as well as the golfers and pool attendees. We consistently feed the many charity golf tournaments as well as private events which include wedding receptions, class reunions & family gatherings throughout the year. As servants of the county, we strive to offer affordable food for all to enjoy and bringing camaraderie to the community.

The Emergency Management Department is responsible for all aspects of disaster management 24 hours a day/seven days a week. We take a “Whole Community Approach’ which is a collaborative effort involving government agencies, non-profit organizations, businesses, and community members. The Emergency Operations Center (EOC) serves as the central hub for communications, command, and coordination for disasters in Walton County and in the EOC we have processes for streamlined resource management, tactical operations, and information coordination with the public and our responding community partners.

The primary function of the County Engineering Department is to manage the design and construction of Walton County infrastructure projects. Additional departmental duties include, but are not limited to, providing capital improvement design and CEI project management (consultants), providing capital improvement construction project management (contractors), traffic operations, right-of-way permitting, surveying, infrastructure (FDOT) grant writing/applications and administration, right-of-way review for development order applications for the Planning Department, plat review for the Planning Department applications, driveway connection permitting to County facilities within municipal boundaries and utility/engineering oversight for the sewer system at the Northwest Florida Commerce Park at Mossy Head. The Engineering Department works with other internal County departments and other County agencies in project management and provides support on grant funded infrastructure improvement projects while coordinating with OMB on grant administration. Project management of County funded capital improvement projects, including in-house projects, is performed by Department staff. Coordination with utility companies, permitting agencies and other project associated parties is facilitated by department staff. The Department provides long range infrastructure programming and coordinates with regional organizations such as the Okaloosa-Walton Transportation Planning Organization. Staff coordinates with Florida Department of Transportation (FDOT), Florida Department of Environmental Protection (FDEP), Northwest Florida Water Management District (NWFWMD), United States Army Corps of Engineers (USACOE) and other State and Federal Agencies that hold regulatory jurisdiction over County projects.

The Walton County Environmental Resource serves as the cornerstone for environmental stewardship within the county, tasked with providing comprehensive environmental support services to various stakeholders including County government, citizens, and federal, state, and local government agencies. At its core, it is dedicated to safeguarding and enhancing the natural resources of Walton County. Through proactive initiatives and collaborative efforts, it addresses a spectrum of environmental issues ranging from conservation and preservation of ecosystems to sustainable development practices. By fostering partnerships and leveraging expertise, the division plays a pivotal role in promoting environmental sustainability, resilience, and harmony between human activities and the natural environment in Walton County.

The Walton County Extension Service (also known as Agricultural Extension Services) provides scientifically based information for current and pertinent issues that will enable county residents and non-residents to make informed decisions that will improve their quality of life. Access of such knowledge is available from the University of Florida and is provided by trained professionals (extension agents). Development of educational programs takes into consideration changes that affect Walton County government, its residents, the environment, and natural and human resources. Local Extension education programs are cooperatively funded by the County, the University of Florida, the U.S. Department of Agriculture, and other joint cooperators.

The Walton County Geographic Information Systems (GIS) Department manages a Geographic Information System and provides geographic services, data, products and resources to multiple users including county offices, other agencies, and the public to aid in decision making.

The Section 8 tenant-based Housing Choice Voucher (HCV) assistance program is funded by the federal government and administered by the Walton County Housing Agency for the jurisdiction of Walton County, Florida. A public housing agency (PHA) is a governmental or public body, created and authorized by state law to develop and operate housing and housing programs for low-income families. The PHA enters into an Annual Contributions Contract with HUD to administer the program requirements on behalf of HUD. The PHA must ensure compliance with federal laws, regulations and notices and must establish policy and procedures to clarify federal requirements and to ensure consistency in program operation.

The Walton County Department of Human Resources provides centralized personnel services for all Walton County BCC departments. We work with departments to identify and assist with workforce issues, including recruitment, selection, performance management, standardizing discipline policies, employee development and knowledge transfer, managing workers’ compensation benefits, and providing ongoing evaluation of workplace policies and procedures. We manage benefits for the Walton County BCC, all constitutional offices, and retirees, including health, dental, vision, life insurance, LTD, optional coverages, and the Florida Retirement System. Furthermore, we oversee ADA compliance issues, including countywide ADA inspections, software conformity, and we respond to ADA concerns brought to the attention of the county. We currently are staffed with 13 full-time employees.

The Public Library System supports free access to library services throughout Walton County with facilities in Flowersview, DeFuniak Springs, Freeport, and Santa Rosa Beach. Additionally, the bookmobile acts as a mobile branch and makes weekly stops along with serving schools, assisted living facilities, and other events in Walton County.

The libraries provide access to items for circulation including books, audiobooks, DVD/Blu-ray, mobile hotspots, Chromebooks, microscopes, telescopes, ukuleles, STEAM kits, StaySharp kits, kids tablets, and other technology equipment. Access to public computers with high-speed internet, WiFi, copying, printing, faxing, and notary are also available.

 
The libraries have maker equipment available for public use, including 3D printers, Glowforge, sewing machines, die cut machines, and robots. Digital resources include the Libby app for e-books, e-audiobooks, and e-magazines, Universal Class for virtual courses on over 600 topics, Knowledge City for professional development and small business courses, CreativeBug for arts and crafts workshops and tutorials, ABCmouse for early literacy learning, and the Florida Electronic Library for Gale databases on many topics of interest.

The libraries offer Interlibrary Loan services, which facilitate borrowing from all libraries in the State of Florida to all of our cardholders. The Walton County Libraries support Career Online High School, providing asynchronous high school diploma programs to adult learners. Additionally, a variety of programs and events for all ages along with one-on-one technology assistance is available at all library locations.

The Mosquito Control Department is dedicated to protecting public health and enhancing the quality of life for residents and visitors by managing mosquito populations. Through strategic planning and targeted interventions, we work to minimize nuisance and reduce the risk of mosquito-borne diseases. Our efforts include surveillance, larval control, and public education, all aimed at achieving effective mosquito management while fostering community involvement and awareness.

The Mossy Head Wastewater Sewer System currently provides gravity and force main sewer service for the Northwest Commerce Industrial Park area. The overall objective for the Mossy Head Wastewater Treatment Facility budget is to ensure the manpower and resources necessary to operate and maintain the plant and wastewater collection system in a cost-effective manner within FDEP operating guidelines, meeting wastewater treatment standards and develop a maintenance schedule for evaluation, routine maintenance and replacement of key components. The Department will utilize the necessary software needed to develop and maintain a modeling program for the wastewater distribution system to analyze current conditions as well as plan for future growth. Coordination efforts with the Surveying Department will continue in order to develop and maintain as-built drawings for the existing sewer system that are needed in the development of the wastewater modeling program. Staff will work, ensure that any new regulatory requirements (FDEP) are being satisfied, identify areas for potential expansion to acquire additional flow to the WWTP necessary to ensure affordable operational costs for users, and further define the system’s usage rate structure for anticipated residential connections in the future and pursue any financial assistance opportunities in regard to any expansion efforts.

The Office of Management and Budget (OMB) plays a pivotal role in Walton County by providing comprehensive financial and administrative support to the Board of County Commissioners (BCC). The department is responsible for overseeing all funds authorized to ensure their proper utilization, and offers advice and guidance to department and division heads. Within the department, key functions include preparing and monitoring the annual operating and capital budget, overseeing grant budgets and reporting, and maintaining the inventory of capital assets. By diligently executing these responsibilities, the OMB contributes significantly to the County’s fiscal responsibility and overall operational efficiency, in alignment with BCC policies and regulatory standards.

Under the direction of the County Attorney, the Office of the County Attorney (OCA) provides legal services to the County. There are three primary areas of focus: contracts, litigation, and public records. Contracts: OCA is responsible for drafting or reviewing all documents that legally bind the County. Litigation: OCA represents the Board in all court cases involving the County, either directly or through facilitating any outside counsel. Public Records: OCA provides records management for the County in addition to supporting and advising all departments to fulfill public records requests (PRR).

The Walton County Planning & Development Services Department serves as staff and provides professional land use planning advice to the Board of County Commissioners. The Department is responsible for implementing, maintaining, and updating the Walton County Comprehensive Plan and Land Development Code, concurrency management, including implementation of the Mobility Plan, Floodplain Management, and management of growth through consistent residential and non-residential development review in unincorporated Walton County to ensure that a proposed development or request is in compliance with the adopted codes, policies, regulations and standards of the County and of other public and quasi-public agencies. The Department also staffs the Planning Commission, the Zoning Board of Adjustments, the Design Review Board, and the Affordable Housing Committee.

Our department's function fulfills a vital role in collaborating with the judicial system to enforce court-ordered obligations for probationers sentenced to county probation. The probation department monitors the progress of probationers to ensure compliance with the various court-ordered conditions.

The Public Works Department provides services related to infrastructure maintenance, repair, and construction that will enhance the quality of life for Walton County citizens and visitors. We go to great lengths to stay abreast of what the concerns of our citizens are, while being mindful of the available taxpayer funds. We diligently consider every infrastructure improvement plan to ensure we are providing the best solutions that will provide a positive, long-term impact.

The Purchasing Department of Walton County plays a crucial role in ensuring the effective and efficient management of purchasing activities in adherence to applicable federal, state, and local laws, statutes, ordinances, regulations, and rules. With a mission centered around optimizing the value for every taxpayer dollar spent, the department is committed to securing goods and services at the most favorable prices while maintaining the highest standards of quality and service delivery. Procurement is also responsible for Inventory Management, ensuring the County maintains adequate supplies of essential items.

The Recreation Department is essential to improving the community’s quality of life by providing safe, well-maintained, and ever-evolving recreational programs. These activities are designed to promote the physical and mental well-being of citizens of all ages, from young children to senior citizens. With a particular emphasis on youth development, the department offers a diverse range of recreational opportunities that foster community engagement, encourage healthy lifestyles, and contribute to the social and cultural enrichment of the area. By prioritizing the needs and interests of its residents, the Recreation Department strives to create a vibrant, active, and connected community.

The Soil Conservation Office of Walton County, in collaboration with the Natural Resources Conservation Service (NRCS), provides technical assistance and financial incentives to help local farmers, ranchers, and foresters practice soil conservation, protect water resources, and create wildlife habitats. This office is essential in implementing voluntary conservation programs that benefit both landowners and the environment. Staffed by soil conservationists and technicians, the office supports the Choctawhatchee River Soil and Water Conservation District by offering USDA-NRCS cost-sharing programs like the Environmental Quality Incentives Program (EQIP) and the Conservation Stewardship Program (CSP). Additionally, the office supplies necessary hydrologic engineering data for designing stormwater and sediment control structures, shares topographical and soil information, maintains historical aerial photos of the county, and guides citizens in connecting with the right conservation agencies.

Walton County Solid Waste (Solid Waste) manages the Franchise Agreement with Waste Management Inc., for municipal waste collection and disposal in Walton County. They also oversee the daily operations of the Walton County Central Landfill (WCCL), which includes a Class I Transfer Station, Class III Landfills, recycling facilities, closed landfill cells, a yard waste facility, a waste tire collection center, and a groundwater monitoring and remediation system. All of these operations are permitted by the Florida Department of Environmental Protection (FDEP). Solid Waste staff are responsible for directing disposal operations, ensuring regulatory compliance, operating waste processing facilities, maintaining the landfill site, roads, stormwater control, and managing the collection and processing of waste and recycling across the county.

The Beach Tram Program is a transportation service designed to improve access to popular beach areas while reducing traffic congestion and parking demand. Funded through tourism revenues, the program provides free shuttle service between designated parking locations and key beach access points, allowing visitors to enjoy a more convenient and efficient beach experience. The initiative supports sustainable tourism by minimizing vehicle impact in high-traffic zones and enhancing overall mobility for residents and guests. It is part of the county’s broader strategy to improve infrastructure, promote accessibility, and elevate the quality of the visitor experience.

Beach Operations encompasses a wide array of critical tasks vital for maintaining the pristine beauty and functionality of our coastal areas. It encompasses not only routine beach maintenance and re-nourishment efforts but also the construction and upkeep of essential infrastructure such as regional and neighborhood beach accesses, bay parks, municipal parking facilities, and the expansive multi-use trail network. Moreover, Beach Operations extends its purview to include the meticulous maintenance of iconic scenic corridors like U.S. Highway 331, U.S. Highway 98, County Route 30A, and the Scenic Gulf Drive Corridor, ensuring these vital routes remain not just conduits of transportation but also scenic treasures reflective of our coastal charm.

Under the Lifeguard Services Agreement with Walton County, the South Walton Fire District receives annual funding to support beach safety operations. Beginning in 2025, the agreement includes a 4% annual increase in compensation based on the prior year’s amount to help sustain service levels as costs rise. This funding structure ensures that lifeguard staffing, training, and equipment needs are met, supporting a safe and enjoyable beach experience for residents and visitors alike.

**Sheriff's Office Beach Safety and Ambassador Programs**

The Walton County Sheriff’s Office oversees a comprehensive beach safety strategy. This includes a dedicated Beach Patrol that provides emergency response, monitors public areas, and ensures a secure environment for residents and visitors alike. In December 2023, the Board of County Commissioners approved the Beach Ambassador Program, staffed by year-round Sheriff’s Office employees. These ambassadors serve as a visible and approachable presence on the beach, focused on proactive engagement, public safety awareness, and enhancing visitor experience through communication and support.

**Beach Code Compliance and Beach Stewards**

Beach Code Compliance Officers patrol beach areas to enforce local regulations and respond to community concerns, ensuring public spaces remain safe, orderly, and accessible. In February 2025, the County approved the Beach Stewardship Program under Code Compliance, allowing for the hiring of two full-time and up to 20 part-time seasonal Beach Stewards. These stewards serve a non-enforcement role, providing visitor education and assistance at regional beach accesses, particularly during the peak season. Their focus is on promoting awareness of beach rules, preserving natural resources, and offering a welcoming presence to guests.

Property tax or Ad valorem taxes are the largest source of revenue for Walton County and result from the levy of taxes on real property and tangible personal property.

Preparation of the proposed ad valorem tax budget utilizes the Property Appraiser's final taxable values, which are typically finalized on the DR-420 (Certificate of Taxable Value) form on July 1. Millage rates are charged against the taxable value to arrive at the total tax on each parcel. One mill equals a $1 tax for each $1,000 of taxable value. 

Property Tax revenues for Walton County have consistently increased, reflecting rising property values due to new construction within the County. The projection for Property taxes is supported by an increase in the County-Wide Certified Taxable Value, rising from $46.5 billion in fiscal year 2026 to $49 billion in fiscal year 2027. In accordance with statutory budgeting practices, the County budgets only 95% of anticipated Property tax collections, providing a conservative estimate that accounts for potential delinquencies and collection variances.

Walton County Tourist Development Tax (TDT) were established in accordance with Florida Statute 125.0104. The Walton County Tourism Department and its related divisions are funded by these taxes collected from visitors on short-term lodging rentals within two distinct TDT districts. The South Walton TDT district collects 5% on short-term rental accommodations located south of the Intracoastal Waterway, while the North Walton TDT district collects 3% on short-term rental accommodations located north of the Intracoastal Waterway.

Tourist Development Tax revenues have seen growth in prior years, resulting from increased tourism. It is projected to remain flat for fiscal year 2027, which is a natural rebalancing as global travel normalizes post-pandemic.

Walton County's discretionary 1-cent small county surtax, authorized under Florida Statute 212.055(3) and established by Ordinance No. 94-16 adopted December 5th, 1994, is the funding mechanism for solid waste collection and disposal throughout the county. This funding source also provides a significant portion of funding for capital projects. The tax is ongoing and does not have a sunset clause.

While revenues from the surtax experienced steady growth over many years, collections have remained relatively flat in recent fiscal years, reflecting a stabilization in consumer spending patterns and economic activity that impacts sales tax revenue. Despite this leveling off, the surtax continues to be a critical source of funding for essential county services and infrastructure investments.

In Walton County, the local option fuel tax, established under Florida Statute 206.41(1)(e) and applied according to Statute 336.025, finances essential transportation and infrastructure projects. The tax is set at five cents per gallon for motor fuel and diesel fuel, with an additional one-cent tax known as the "ninth cent." These funds are used for maintaining and repairing county roads and bridges, enhancing traffic safety, and improving public transportation. This revenue ensures that transportation remains safe, reliable, and efficient for both residents and visitors, supporting the county's growth and development. According to Florida Statute 336.025, counties can impose this local option fuel tax for up to ten years, meaning it will need to be renewed in 2028 to continue its benefits.

The Local Option Fuel Tax and Ninth Cent Tax have maintained a relatively stable revenue stream, with minor fluctuations. This stability underscores consistent fuel consumption and reliable tax collection efforts.

This program allocates a half-cent of the state's sales tax to local governments, supporting infrastructure projects, public safety, parks, and other essential services. The funds, distributed monthly, enable local governments to enhance community services and facilities, fostering improved quality of life across the state.

The Local Government 1/2 Cent Sales Tax has shown steady growth over the years, with significant peaks during the summer months reflecting strong economic activity. It is projected to remain flat in fiscal year 2027 due to inflationary pressure and stabilized consumer spending.

The Florida Revenue Sharing Act of 1972 was a significant legislative effort to ensure a minimum level of revenue parity across local government units. An allocation formula is used to distribute 2.9 percent of net cigarette tax collections and 2.044 percent of sales and use tax collections among qualifying counties. This formula considers each county's total population, unincorporated population, and sales tax collections to determine its share.

State Revenue Share Proceeds have generally increased over time, but the most recent year showed a slight decline. This suggests that revenues may be stabilizing, reflecting a potential plateau in the underlying economic activity that drives these distributions.

Walton County receives federal funding through the Section 8 Housing Choice Voucher (HCV) Program, administered by the Walton County Housing Agency under contract with the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD).

These funds support rental assistance for eligible low-income families and help cover administrative functions such as application review, eligibility verification, housing inspections, and ongoing compliance monitoring. The program is operated under an Annual Contributions Contract with HUD, with all revenue restricted to eligible housing activities defined by federal regulations.

This funding plays a key role in expanding access to affordable housing in Walton County and supporting the day-to-day operations of the local Housing Agency. Annual revenues fluctuate based on federal appropriations and local demand.

In accordance with the contractual agreements between the Walton County Sheriff’s Office and the Walton County School District, funds are received from the District to support the Sheriff’s Office in providing School Resource Officers (SROs) at schools throughout the county. This revenue ensures that the Sheriff’s Office can fulfill its obligations under the agreement, maintaining trained personnel and necessary resources to promote a safe and secure learning environment for students and staff.

The remaining revenues within the Intergovernmental Revenue category consist of various state-shared and state-distributed funds. These include revenues from the state-shared cigarette tax, alcoholic beverage licenses, E911 communication taxes, insurance agent license fees, mobile home licenses, racing or gambling tax proceeds, state payments in lieu of taxes, and state aid for mosquito control. These state-distributed revenues help support essential county operations and public services, enhancing Walton County’s ability to meet community needs.

Narrative:
Eagle Springs revenue is generated through various recreation-based fees, including green fees, cart fees, membership dues, pro shop sales, and food and beverage services. These revenues support the daily operations of the course, helping to fund staffing, maintenance, and overall facility upkeep.

Revenue has increased in recent years due to both higher participation and scheduled fee increases that reflect the growing popularity of the course's amenities. Membership and green fee revenues in particular have seen consistent growth, driven by increased community usage and demand for recreational services.

This funding stream is essential for maintaining the quality of services and ensuring that park users continue to benefit from well-managed and well-maintained facilities. Projections for FY 2025 and FY 2026 reflect this upward trend, with budgets adjusted to account for both historical performance and continued demand.

Ambulance fee revenue is collected through the provision of emergency medical transport services within Walton County. These fees are billed to patients or their insurance providers following transport by EMS personnel.

Revenue generated from ambulance services is deposited into the Fine and Forfeiture Fund, where it directly supports the operations of Walton County Sheriff Fire Rescue. This includes funding for personnel, vehicles, medical equipment, and other essential resources required to deliver timely and effective emergency response.

The Walton County Fire Rescue Municipal Service Benefit Unit (MSBU) is a vital funding mechanism established to support fire rescue services, facilities, and programs throughout the county. The assessment rates for residential properties are set at $75.00 per dwelling unit, while non-residential properties are charged based on their usage category: $0.12 per square foot for commercial, $0.01 for industrial/warehouse, and $0.12 for institutional properties. Land properties, such as agricultural or vacant land, are assessed at a rate of $0.07 per acre.

The Fire Rescue MSBU revenues have remained stable, showing a steady collection of assessments for fire rescue services.

The remaining revenue in the Charges for Services category includes revenues collected by the County in exchange for specific services provided to the public. These revenues consist of animal shelter fees, public records fees, cremation fees, the $2 court recording fee, landfill fees, library fees, lien search fees, prisoner housing revenue, and the $65 fee established under Florida Statute 939.185. Revenue from building permits is generated from fees collected for the issuance of permits required for new construction, renovations, and various building projects. Interest is the income earned from the county's investments, such as certificates of deposit (CDs), money market funds, and bonds. These investments generate interest by lending our funds to financial institutions or entities, which then pay us for using that money. Our largest interest revenue comes from Corporate Bonds and other similar investments.

The Sidewalk Fund accounts for assessments charged to developers in lieu of construction of sidewalks as required by the Walton County Land Development Code. Budgeted expenditures within the Sidewalk fund are used for the construction or repair of sidewalks or multi use paths within Walton County.

The E911 fund accounts for phone charges assessed for the purpose of providing emergency assistance. E911 is a system used in North America that links emergency callers with the appropriate public resources within that geographic area. The State of Florida requires E911 receipts to be maintained in a separate general ledger fund. These funds are transferred to the Sheriff’s fund to be used for E911 expenditures and are included in the Sheriff’s overall budget total.

Chapter 125.01(q) 1 of the Florida Statutes authorizes the Board of County Commissioners (BCC) to create or abolish an MSBU. The law permits such districts to be created for the purpose of providing and maintaining facilities or services (such as fire services) which specifically benefit property owners in a particular area. The facilities or services must provide a public purpose. Chapter 197.3632 of the Florida Statutes provides for the levy, collection, and enforcement of non-ad valorem assessments through the uniform method.

The initiation of a MSBU can be requested by property owners in the unincorporated area of Walton County.  Municipal Service Benefit Unit improvements can include potable water, sanitary sewer, reuse water, roadway paving, canal dredging, or drainage improvements. This public service must be approved by the Board of County Commissioners. The main purpose of this program is to retrofit existing developments with an improvement that at least 66.66% of the affected property owners have requested and approved. The MSBU improvements are funded by service charges, special assessments, or taxes within the MSBU for the cost of the improvements.

Following the finalization and acceptance of the project by the Board of County Commissioners, affected owners have a 30-day period to pay any part or all of the special assessment charge with no interest. If payment in full is not received, interest will accrue on a monthly basis following the 30-day period. The annual billing for the special assessment takes place in November of each year. The bill will include the annual principal payment plus accrued interest. The installment payment must be made by December 31st of each year to prevent additional interest/penalties from accruing on the special assessment account.

The MSBU, or Municipal Service Benefit Unit, Fund accounts for special assessments charged to various property owners to provide for infrastructure within that specific geographic area. A Municipal Services Benefit Unit is a non-ad valorem assessment district established to provide funding for improvements in a specific geographic area within the county.
